newsitem.title: USA: Weld relinquishes power for diplomatic quest.
newsitem.headline: Weld relinquishes power for diplomatic quest.

text.p: William Weld took his last walk down the red-carpeted State House steps as governor of Massachusetts on Tuesday and formally handed the office to now acting Gov. Paul Cellucci.
Under a brilliantly clear sky, cannons on the Boston Commons fired a 19-gun salute as Weld met Cellucci half way up the ceremonial steps. The two shook hands and he continued down as citizen Weld.

On Thursday, his 52nd birthday, the fiscal conservative and socially liberal Weld will climb Washington's Capitol steps and try to convince fellow Republican Sen. Jesse Helms to hold hearings on his nomination as U.S. ambassador to Mexico.
Helms, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, has refused to grant Weld a hearing, ostensibly on grounds that he was "soft on drugs" and not of ambassadorial calibre.
Weld may have sealed his fate when he accused Helms of "ideological extortion" and challenged moderate Republicans to rise up against the powerful North Carolina senator.

But Helms appeared unmoved by Weld's resignation. On Monday, a spokesman for the senator said the panel had not seen a "nominee conduct himself this way before. "This is just a PR stunt for the governor, and we wish him luck."
New England Republican Sens. John Chaffee of Rhode Island and Olympia Snowe of Maine circulated a letter among their colleagues on Weld's behalf to drum up support for hearings.

On his last day in office, Weld met with his staff and legislators and then turned over to Cellucci the key to the govenor's office, a 100-year-old Bible, a gavel from the USS Constitution and some Indian arrowheads.

At the end of the State House steps, Weld got behind the wheel of his Chevy Blazer with his wife and three of his six children in the car and drove off, leaving behind a state trooper who had been his chauffeur, hundreds of onlookers and Cellucci.

Under the state constitution, Cellucci, also a Republican, becomes acting governor and retains the title of lieutenant governor. Not too much is expected to change in the next 18 months under a Cellucci administration and it gives the 49-year-old career politician a chance to prove to the voters he should be elected to the office on his own.

"Paul Cellucci helped Bill Weld become a good governor by explaining how to be a moderate. I think to a great extent this is the way that Weld had always intended to pay him back, always in the hope that he would in fact help him become governor after they had had such a successful run," said political analyst Lou DiNatale.
